transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
FBI personnel who were fired after participating
in the Bureau's investigation of President Trump's handling
of classified documents following his first term
are now suing to get their jobs back.
Their lawsuit was filed in federal court in Washington
on behalf of nine agents, intelligence analysts,
and staff operations specialists.
FBI Director Kash Patel has testified in Congress
that the people he fired had weaponized the Bureau.
Patients may soon no longer have the option
of buying their prescription drugs
from Canadian pharmacies to save money.
And Pierre Sidney Lupkin reports on coming changes
to import rules.
The U.S. allows people to import a 90-day supply
of pharmaceuticals with a prescription from a doctor
under certain conditions.
And the medicines pass through customs fairly easily
as long as they are valued below $800.
But a rule change at U.S. Customs and Border Protection
would require more paperwork, a broker,
and something called an entry bond.
That would make the practice more expensive
or even impossible for the estimated 2 million patients
who import medicines for personal use.
The change was originally set to take effect next week
but has been pushed back to January of next year.
Sydney Lupkin, NPR News.
A U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity
tells NPR, "President Trump was talked out
of a livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hassan
based on two reasons.
It's against American values to televise an execution,
and there was a concern that the tape would show up
on Jihadi websites, leading to an increase in recruits
as well as possible danger to U.S. forces
in the Middle East region in particular."
In addition, a U.S. official on Capitol Hill
who was not authorized to speak publicly
told NPR that it was Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
who called for the firing squad to be televised.
The official said the idea, quote,
"Caught everyone by surprise."
Rising inflation in the U.S. is adding to the strain
on household budgets, and PR's Windsor-Johnson
tells his people across the country,
"Have collectively spent about $82 billion more
on gasoline since March than they did a year ago."
That estimate comes from the latest calculation
by GasBuddy.com. Patrick DeHaan is head of petroleum analysis.
He says those extra fuel expenses are leaving families
with less to spend on holiday meals and gifts.
He also says booking holiday flights now won't spare
travelers from higher fuel costs.
"The airlines are having to pass this along,
so you can't avoid the increase in fuel when
what comes out of a barrel is fueling the entire U.S. economy.
You can't escape it."
Heavy, bulky goods, including Thanksgiving turkeys
and perishable foods, are especially vulnerable
to higher shipping costs. Windsor-Johnson, NPR News.
This is NPR.
While the U.S. economy weighs on voters
in the run-up to the midterm elections,
President Trump is back at the White House
after a wave of midterm campaign stops across the country,
and Piers Tamara Keith reports.
"Most of these stops aren't just about feeling
the warm embrace of an adoring rally crowd.
The map of competitive House and Senate races
includes a lot of states and districts Trump won
by healthy margins just two years ago.
Republicans are playing defense in Alaska, Texas, Iowa, Ohio,
and now even Kansas."
NPR's Tamara Keith reporting.
Scientists say elephants have an outsized effect
on landscapes both in life and death,
and PR's Alana Gordon reports.
"Elephants are ecosystem engineers.
They knock down trees, they disperse seeds,
but scientists in South Africa's Kruger National Park
found something they didn't expect after the animals die.
The group monitored dozens of elephant carcasses
on the savannah and found that over time,
the remains created unique nutrient-rich hot spots
for certain grasses.
This drew animals like zebras and antelope
well after any visual signs of the elephant had disappeared.
Courtney Reed is with UC Santa Barbara in Princeton.
She led the research.
"Seeing that even like eight years on,
you have all of these different herbivores
that live on the savannah that are really selecting
for those nitrogen-rich grasses.
It was just exciting."
Reed says this lasting legacy highlights
the importance of elephants as they face threats of extinction.
The findings were published in the proceedings
of the National Academy of Sciences.
Alana Gordon, NPR News.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.

topics.text: FBI agents fired over Trump classified documents probe sue to win their jobs back
Patients may lose option to import prescription drugs from Canadian pharmacies under new customs rule
Trump reportedly talked out of livestreaming Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's execution, official says
Americans have spent about $82 billion more on gasoline since March, GasBuddy says
Trump returns to White House after midterm campaign stops as Republicans defend competitive districts
Kruger National Park study finds dead elephants create lasting nutrient hot spots for grasses
